intro: Wagner wrote the Siegfried Idyll, WWV 103, as a birthday greeting for Cosima; it opens with a long violin melody and includes a lullaby, a horn call and the song of a bird. Stanley Chapple conducted the Modern Chamber Orchestra in this 1925 recording.

sections.label: A · Violin phrase in E major
sections.mNote: A violin plays a long E-major phrase; other strings join.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme, strings and wind
sections.mNote: Strings and wind share the long melody.

sections.label: B · Oboe lullaby melody
sections.mNote: The oboe plays the melody above short detached string figures.

sections.label: Dev · Horn and clarinet melodies
sections.mNote: Wind melodies cross the flowing lines of the strings

sections.label: C · Horn theme with woodwind calls
sections.mNote: The horn plays a song theme against quick clarinet and flute calls.

sections.label: A″ · The long melody returns
sections.mNote: The opening string melody returns among the other melodies.

sections.label: Coda · Strings and horn over E
sections.mNote: Strings and a low horn hold E.

cues.title: Opening, successive string entries
cues.text: The first violins begin alone, softly, Ruhig bewegt. Violas and cellos enter beneath the held note, then the second violins add a moving line. The double bass rests.
cues.evidence: Wagner, Siegfried-Idyll, Schott full score, 1878, plate 22430, p. 1: Ruhig bewegt, successive string entries, double bass silent. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/20380.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Tribschen, 1870
cues.text: On Christmas morning, 1870, thirteen musicians played on the stairs at Tribschen while Cosima woke upstairs. “Music was sounding, and such music,” she wrote in her diary. When it ended, Wagner came in with the five children and gave her the score.
cues.evidence: Cosima Wagner’s diary, 25 December 1870, English extract in the Verdehr Trio programme note: https://verdehr.com/notes-WagnerSiegfriedIdyll.pdf. Gerald Larner identifies the thirteen players and staircase: https://geraldlarner.com/work/wagner-siegfried-idyll.

cues.title: String quartet for Cosima, 1864
cues.text: Wagner first sketched the opening melody in 1864 for a string quartet for Cosima. He never finished the quartet. The tune went into Brünnhilde’s music in Siegfried, and later into this family greeting.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, Siegfried Idyll programme note: the projected 1864 quartet, its dedication to Cosima, and the theme’s later use in Siegfried, Act III. https://geraldlarner.com/work/wagner-siegfried-idyll.

cues.title: Oboe lullaby, Sehr einfach
cues.text: Wagner marks the oboe’s lullaby Sehr einfach (“very simply”). Its short phrases sit above detached notes in the violins, then in the lower strings.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, p. 12, oboe entry marked Sehr einfach and detached string accompaniment. Gerald Larner identifies the traditional German lullaby and its association with Wagner’s daughter Eva.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening theme and lullaby combined
cues.text: Through the middle span the melodies overlap. A wind instrument holds a phrase while a string line moves beneath it, and fragments of the opening theme are fitted around the lullaby. On p. 24 of the Schott full score, horn, clarinet and strings play independent lines.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, middle span, including p. 24: horn, clarinet and independent string lines. Gerald Larner describes the combination and inversion of the opening theme and lullaby. This note concerns the recurring counterpoint, not a single entrance.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Original title
cues.text: The original title was Tribschener Idyll mit Fidi-Vogelgesang und Orange-Sonnenaufgang (Tribschen Idyll with Fidi’s Birdsong and Orange Sunrise). Fidi was the family’s nickname for their son Siegfried, born in June 1869. The name Siegfried Idyll refers both to the son and to the opera.
cues.evidence: Rainer Fineske, for the International Association of Wagner Societies, on the work’s 150th anniversary: the original title, Fidi as Siegfried, and the link with the opera; Siegfried’s birth on 6 June 1869 in the Richard Wagner Museum’s account of the Tribschen years. https://www.richard-wagner.org/rwvi/en/news/news-committee/?collection_id=3075 https://www.richard-wagner-museum.ch/en/museum/years-in-lucerne/

cues.title: Horn theme and Woodbird figures
cues.text: The horn plays Siegfried’s tune in C major. Clarinet and flute follow with quick Woodbird figures from Siegfried, marked lustig — merrily.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, pp. 28–29: Lebhaft in C major, horn melody followed by clarinet and flute figures marked lustig. The operatic themes are identified in Gerald Larner’s programme note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sale to Schott, 1878
cues.text: Under financial pressure, Wagner sold the Idyll to Schott. The full score was published in 1878. The work had first been played on a staircase.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner on the sale under financial pressure: https://geraldlarner.com/work/wagner-siegfried-idyll. Schott’s first full-score edition is dated 1878 in the Sibley catalogue: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/20380.

cues.title: Hans Richter, witness and trumpeter
cues.text: On 25 August 1870, four months before the staircase, Wagner and Cosima married; Hans Richter was one of the two witnesses. Richter, Wagner’s copyist, learned the trumpet specially for the birthday performance. The trumpet part lasts thirteen bars.
cues.evidence: Richard Wagner Museum, Lucerne: the wedding of 25 August 1870 and its witnesses, Malwida von Meysenbug and Hans Richter. Richter as Wagner’s copyist and the trumpeter of the first performance: Mahler Foundation biography. He learned the trumpet for the occasion: Concise Oxford Dictionary of Music. A trumpet part of only 13 bars: Rainer Fineske, International Association of Wagner Societies. https://www.richard-wagner-museum.ch/en/museum/years-in-lucerne/ https://www.mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/contemporaries/hans-richter https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/siegfried-idyll https://www.richard-wagner.org/rwvi/en/news/news-committee/?collection_id=3075

cues.title: Closing bars, sustained bass E
cues.text: The double bass holds E, with a low note in the second horn, while the strings play short final figures. The wind players, silent until now, enter pianissimo on the final chord of E major, which carries a fermata.
cues.evidence: Schott full score, p. 46: sustained E in double bass and second horn, moving string fragments, final pp wind entry and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Oboe enters with the lullaby
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme, strings and wind
transitions.how: The horns finish their phrase and stop. Over a few pizzicato bass notes, the strings play a link marked diminuendo, leading to the B-major lullaby. The oboe enters, marked Sehr einfach, over detached violin figures. Soon afterwards the bass rests.
transitions.evidence: Schott full score, p. 12: diminuendo, pizzicato bass, oboe Sehr einfach and detached violin accompaniment. The recording’s section boundary locates the approach to this passage.

transitions.title: Change to Lebhaft and horn duet
transitions.to: C · Horn theme with woodwind calls
transitions.how: The flute and violins finish their quick descending figures. Wagner removes the strings and marks the new section Lebhaft, in C major. One horn holds the bass beneath the other’s melody. The clarinet and flute then enter with the Woodbird’s quick triplets.
transitions.evidence: Schott full score, pp. 28–29, change to Lebhaft, horn duet and subsequent clarinet and flute entries.

transitions.title: Rallentando to the E pedal
transitions.to: Coda · Strings and horn over E
transitions.how: The last string phrases slow, first with a Rallentando, then at Bedeutend langsamer (considerably slower). A low horn holds E and the double bass takes up the same pedal. Fragments of the melody continue above it in the strings, marked immer pp.
transitions.evidence: Schott full score, pp. 45–46. The named markings and E pedal belong to the closing section; the section boundary marks its approach.

source.title: Siegfried-Idyll — Schott full score, 1878, plate 22430
source.locator: Printed pp. 1, 4, 8, 12, 24, 28, 31–32, 36, 45–46. Approximate score regions; the 1925 session’s exact staffing is not documented.

timeline.note: Opening string span, p. 1; basses and winds are initially silent in the published score.
Approximate opening expansion, pp. 4–8: woodwinds, horns and basses progressively join the string texture. The 1:06 audio boundary marks the broad region, not simultaneous or bar-aligned entrances.
Approximate contrasting-song region, p. 12: the oboe enters with the lullaby over a reduced texture.
Approximate combination region, p. 24: horn line, clarinet support and moving strings.
Approximate animated region, p. 28: horn call and flute forest-bird figure; these are not simultaneous throughout the span.
Central stronger region, pp. 31–32. Trumpet reinforcement is brief and does not cover the entire span.
Approximate later recollection, p. 36: light wind exchanges above returning string movement.
Closing region, pp. 45–46: horn and bassoon support the sustained strings. Flute, oboe and clarinets enter only for the final chord; the trumpet does not play.

composer.epithet: Composer who placed the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth, hidden from the audience.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no real success. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons playing against the storm music in the strings. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to get his music staged.

He grew up in the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. He heard Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies, and in 1831 he took counterpoint lessons from Theodor Weinlig. Posts followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen was not performed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, failed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
